cue: When does the Christmas season actually start?

es.meaning: Mexican colloquial name for the stretch from 12 December (Virgin of Guadalupe) to 6 January (Three Kings): almost four weeks of posadas, parties, and eating, joked about as an endurance event.
es.example: Ya empezó el maratón Guadalupe-Reyes y no he parado de comer tamales.
es.exampleTranslation: The Guadalupe-Reyes marathon has started and I haven't stopped eating tamales.
es.regionNote: A Mexican expression; elsewhere the dates mean little as a pair.

it.literal: from the Immaculate Conception to Epiphany
it.meaning: The traditional span of the Italian Christmas season: the tree and presepe go up on 8 December, a national holiday, and come down after 6 January.
it.example: Da noi l'albero si fa all'Immacolata e si smonta dopo l'Epifania.
it.exampleTranslation: At our house the tree goes up on the Immacolata and comes down after Epiphany.

bridge.note: Both countries bracket the season between two church feasts and both end on 6 January, but they start in different places and frame it differently. Italy opens on 8 December, the Immaculate Conception, a national holiday and the customary day to put up the tree. Mexico opens four days later on 12 December, the feast of the Virgin of Guadalupe, the country's most-visited pilgrimage day, and calls the whole run a 'maratón', a joke about stamina rather than a devotional label. Spanish Spain also keeps 8 December as a holiday, so the Guadalupe start is specifically Mexican.

interference.es_to_it: A Mexican speaker who expects the season to start on the 12th will find Italian homes already decorated and offices already closed once, on the 8th.
interference.it_to_es: An Italian hearing 'maratón Guadalupe-Reyes' may take it as a religious calendar term; it is a joke about how much partying the four weeks involve.
